title: Which is dearer?
hookLine: fame or your life, which is dearer? know contentment and avoid disgrace (Tao Te Ching 44)

cards: Late at night, a phone lights up a face in a dark room. Refresh. How many people saw the post?
Refresh. Did anyone new follow? An hour goes by that could have been sleep, or a talk with someone in the next room, or nothing at all.
Nobody chose to trade the hour. It just went. Chapter forty-four of the Tao Te Ching doesn't scold anyone for this.
It asks a question instead, and leaves it standing there.

teach.b: First, the question. James Legge set chapter forty-four in rhyme, and it opens: "Or fame or life, Which do you hold more dear? Or life or wealth, To which would you adhere?" The chapter doesn't answer for you.
Second, the trade. Great attachment, it says, brings great cost, and piling things up leads to heavy loss. It isn't saying a name or money is evil.

teach.h: WHAT YOU SPEND TO GET IT.
teach.b: It's pointing at the trade underneath: what you spend of your actual life to get them. Third, the way out it offers. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace.
Whoever knows when to stop avoids danger, and can last a long time. Those aren't prizes at the end. They're the brakes on the trade.

Fourth, fame at a small scale. It can be a few more likes, the boss's notice, being the one who always says yes. Each of those costs something: an evening, an hour of sleep, a weekend with someone you love.
The question isn't a rule. It's a weighing.
And this is the end of a week, so here is what it gathered: without trying, rooted low, returning, they laugh, carry both, the softest, and today, which is dearer.
Small, quiet strengths that can look like weakness from outside.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often use chapter forty-four's question, fame or life, as a check on chasing recognition or money at the cost of health, rest and the people around them.

o: asking which person in your life you love most
asking which of two things costs more money
the question of whether fame or your life matters more

p: which do you hold more dear?

s: chapter forty-four says money and a name are evil
it points at the trade: what you spend of your life to get them.
the chapter opens with questions it doesn't answer for you
fame or life, which is dearer? life or wealth?
in the chapter, whoever knows when to stop can last a long time
knowing when to stop avoids danger.

games.q: it's midnight, and you could check how your post did one more time. what does chapter forty-four ask?
o: which is dearer, this or your life?
games.why: the chapter asks: fame or life, which do you hold more dear? it leaves the answer to you.

practice: Let one small chase come to mind, something you do to be seen, praised or counted, and hold it in one hand. In the other, hold what it costs: sleep, time with someone, quiet, your attention.
Don't decide anything yet; just feel the weight in each hand.

wordCard.voice: Which is dearer? Chapter forty-four's question: fame or your life, wealth or your life. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: name, fame; the first word of chapter forty-four's question.

carryVoice: Your line: which is dearer. A question to hold, not a rule to keep. That's the week.
